summary: Specifies Geneve, a generic encapsulation for network virtualization. Tunnel needs vary because the devices involved, such as software and hardware tunnel endpoints and central control, differ widely, so Geneve is designed to be flexible and extensible. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: Virtual networks need to add an outer header to their messages so they can travel across a real network. Geneve is a flexible design for that header, and it works with many different kinds of equipment.

questions: how big is the geneve header
subtitle: A flexible tunnel header with room for extensible metadata, built to carry virtual networks across ordinary IP data center fabrics.

tldr.problem: Network virtualization needs tunnels that can carry more metadata than a 24-bit identifier and that keep up with changing control planes, hypervisor switches, hardware and middleboxes.
tldr.mechanism: Geneve wraps the original packet in UDP over IPv4 or IPv6, behind a small fixed 8-byte header that carries a 24-bit Virtual Network Identifier, followed by optional Type-Length-Value options that tunnel endpoints define and interpret.
tldr.outcome: Geneve is a Proposed Standard that defines only the data plane and leaves the control plane open, so it can replace or coexist with VXLAN and NVGRE. Its security rests on isolating the underlay or adding IPsec-style protection.

today: RFC 8926 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2020, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sits alongside the earlier VXLAN and NVGRE encapsulations, which the RFC expects Geneve to coexist with during any transition.

sections.title: Why Another Encapsulation
sections.content:
Networking has long featured a variety of tunneling, tagging and other encapsulation mechanisms, but the advent of network virtualization has caused a surge of renewed interest and a corresponding increase in the introduction of new protocols, ranging from VLANs and MPLS through the more recent VXLAN (RFC 7348) and NVGRE (RFC 7637).

While many encapsulation protocols seek only to partition the underlay network or bridge two domains, network virtualization views the transit network as providing connectivity between multiple components of a distributed system. In many ways this system is similar to a chassis switch, with the IP underlay network playing the role of the backplane and the tunnel endpoints on the edge as line cards. Viewed in this light, the requirements on the tunneling protocol are significantly different in terms of the quantity of metadata necessary and the role of transit nodes.

One additional defining requirement of network virtualization is the need to carry metadata, such as system state, along with the packet data. Nearly all protocols used for network virtualization have at least 24 bits of identifier space as a way to partition between tenants, and 16 million possible entries is a large number for a tenant identifier. The reality, however, is that the metadata is not exclusively used to identify tenants, and encoding other information quickly starts to crowd the space. Compared with the tags used to exchange metadata between line cards on a chassis switch, 24-bit identifiers start to look quite small. There are nearly endless uses for this metadata, from storing input port identifiers for simple security policies to sending service-based context for advanced middlebox applications that terminate and re-encapsulate Geneve traffic.

Existing tunneling protocols have each attempted to solve different aspects of these new requirements, only to be quickly rendered out of date by changing control plane implementations and advancements. Geneve seeks to avoid these problems by providing a framework for tunneling for network virtualization rather than being prescriptive about the entire system.
sections.plainLanguage: Virtual networks need to wrap their messages in an outer envelope so they can travel across a real network. Geneve is a flexible envelope design that works for many different kinds of equipment.

sections.title: Design Requirements
sections.content:
Geneve is designed to support network virtualization use cases for data center environments. Tunnels are typically established to act as a backplane between the virtual switches residing in hypervisors, physical switches, middleboxes or other appliances. An arbitrary IP network can be used as an underlay, although Clos networks composed using ECMP links are a common choice to provide consistent bisectional bandwidth across all connection points.

To support the needs of network virtualization, the tunneling protocol should be able to take advantage of the differing and evolving capabilities of each type of device in both the underlay and overlay networks. This results in three requirements on the data plane tunneling protocol: the data plane must be generic and extensible enough to support current and future control planes; tunnel components must be efficiently implementable in both hardware and software without restricting capabilities to the lowest common denominator; and high performance over existing IP fabrics must be maintained.

Control plane independence. Some protocols have included a control plane in the tunnel format specification, most notably VXLAN, which prescribed a multicast-learning-based control plane, but those specifications have largely been treated as describing only the data format, and the VXLAN packet format has seen a wide variety of control planes built on top of it. Control planes, by contrast, are diverse in very fundamental ways, so the case for standardization is less clear. Geneve is therefore a pure tunnel format specification that is capable of fulfilling the needs of many control planes by explicitly not selecting any one of them, which promotes a shared data format and reduces the chance of obsolescence.

Data plane extensibility. Achieving the needed flexibility requires an options infrastructure, so that new metadata types can be defined, deployed, and either finalized or retired. Options are equally important in data packets as in control packets, for segregating and directing forwarding.

Use of standard IP fabrics. Nearly all underlay fabrics exploit parallelism in traffic, using ECMP techniques that hash the addresses and port numbers of the packet to select an outgoing link. The use of tunnels often results in poor ECMP performance, because the encapsulated traffic is hidden from the fabric by design and only tunnel endpoint addresses are available for hashing. Entropy from encapsulated packets must therefore be exposed in the tunnel header, and the most common technique is to use the UDP source port.
sections.plainLanguage: The design has three goals: do not pick a control plane, leave room for new metadata, and keep the traffic spread evenly across the links of the underlay network.

sections.title: Packet Layout and the UDP Header
sections.content:
The Geneve packet format consists of a compact tunnel header encapsulated in UDP over either IPv4 or IPv6. A small fixed tunnel header provides control information plus a base level of functionality and interoperability, with a focus on simplicity. It is followed by a set of variable-length options to allow for future innovation. Finally, the payload consists of a protocol data unit of the indicated type, such as an Ethernet frame. The original frame's preamble, start frame delimiter and frame check sequence are not included, and the Ethernet payload need not be 4-byte aligned.

The use of an encapsulating UDP header follows the connectionless semantics of Ethernet and IP, in addition to providing entropy to routers performing ECMP. The source port is selected by the originating tunnel endpoint and SHOULD be the same for all packets belonging to a single encapsulated flow, to prevent reordering due to the use of different paths. It SHOULD be calculated using a hash of the encapsulated packet headers, for example a traditional 5-tuple, and because the port represents a flow identifier rather than a true UDP connection, the entire 16-bit range MAY be used to maximize entropy. For IPv6 the flow label MAY also be used for entropy.

IANA has assigned port 6081 as the fixed well-known destination port for Geneve. Although the well-known value should be used by default, it is RECOMMENDED that implementations make this configurable. The chosen port is used for identification of Geneve packets and MUST NOT be reversed for different ends of a connection, as is done with TCP. The UDP length is the length of the UDP packet including the UDP header.

To protect the Geneve header, options and payload from data corruption, the UDP checksum SHOULD be generated when Geneve is encapsulated in IPv4, and MUST be generated by default when it is encapsulated in IPv6. A receiver that gets a packet with a non-zero UDP checksum MUST validate it: if the checksum is not correct the packet MUST be dropped, and otherwise it MUST be accepted for decapsulation.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel is a small fixed header, then any number of options, then the original packet. It rides in UDP so that the fabric can spread traffic over many links, using the source port to do the hashing.

sections.title: The Tunnel Header Fields
sections.content:
The Ver field is 2 bits and the current version number is 0. Packets received by a tunnel endpoint with an unknown version MUST be dropped, and transit devices interpreting Geneve packets with an unknown version number MUST treat them as UDP packets with an unknown payload.

The Opt Len field is 6 bits and gives the length of the option fields expressed in 4-byte multiples, not including the 8-byte fixed tunnel header. This results in a minimum total Geneve header size of 8 bytes and a maximum of 260 bytes. Transit devices MUST maintain consistent forwarding behavior irrespective of the value of Opt Len, including ECMP link selection.

The O bit is 1 bit and marks a control packet, which contains a control message sent between tunnel endpoints. Tunnel endpoints MUST NOT forward the payload, and transit devices MUST NOT attempt to interpret it. Since control messages are less frequent, it is RECOMMENDED that tunnel endpoints direct these packets to a high-priority control queue. Transit devices MUST NOT alter forwarding behavior on the basis of this bit.

The C bit is 1 bit and marks critical options present. If it is set, tunnel endpoints MUST parse the options list to interpret any critical options, and on tunnel endpoints where option parsing is not supported the packet MUST be dropped on the basis of the C bit. If the bit is not set, tunnel endpoints MAY strip all options and forward the decapsulated packet. Transit devices MUST NOT drop packets on the basis of this bit. The Rsvd field is 6 bits, MUST be zero on transmission and MUST be ignored on receipt.

The Protocol Type field is 16 bits and gives the type of protocol data unit appearing after the Geneve header, following the Ethertype convention, with Ethernet itself represented by the value 0x6558. The Virtual Network Identifier is 24 bits and is an identifier for a unique element of a virtual network. In many situations this may represent an L2 segment, but the control plane defines the forwarding semantics of decapsulated packets, and the VNI MAY be used as part of ECMP forwarding decisions or to distinguish between overlapping address spaces when load balancing across CPUs. A final Reserved field of 8 bits MUST be zero on transmission and is ignored on receipt.
sections.plainLanguage: The fixed part of the header is 64 bits. Two bits say which version of the protocol this is, six say how long the options are, one says whether this is a control packet, one says whether there are options the receiver must understand, and the rest carry the virtual network identifier and the type of the payload.

sections.title: Tunnel Options
sections.content:
The base Geneve header is followed by zero or more options in Type-Length-Value format. Each option consists of a 4-byte option header and a variable amount of option data interpreted according to the type.

The Option Class field is 16 bits and is the namespace for the Type field. IANA has created a 'Geneve Option Class' registry to allocate identifiers for organizations, technologies and vendors that have an interest in creating types for options, and each organization may allocate types independently to allow experimentation and rapid innovation. Certain ranges are reserved for allocation by IETF Review and for Experimental Use.

The Type field is 8 bits and indicates the format of the data contained in the option. Its high-order bit indicates that this is a critical option: if the receiving tunnel endpoint does not recognize the option and the bit is set, the packet MUST be dropped, and if the bit is set in any option then the C bit in the Geneve base header MUST also be set. Transit devices MUST NOT drop packets on the basis of this bit. The requirement to drop a packet with an unknown critical option applies to the tunnel endpoint system as a whole, so in a system made of a forwarding ASIC and a general purpose CPU the packet does not have to be dropped in the ASIC; an implementation may send it to the CPU over a rate-limited control channel.

The R field is 3 bits of option control flags reserved for future use, which MUST be zero on transmission and MUST be ignored on receipt. The Length field is 5 bits and gives the length of the option in 4-byte multiples, excluding the option header, so the total length of each option may be between 4 and 128 bytes. A value of 0 in the Length field implies an option with only an option header and no option data. Packets in which the total length of all options is not equal to the Opt Len in the base header are invalid and MUST be silently dropped by a tunnel endpoint that processes the options.
sections.plainLanguage: Options are the part of the tunnel that can grow over time. Each one has a class that says who owns it, a type that says what it means, and a length. An option can be marked critical, which means a receiver that does not understand it has to drop the packet.

sections.title: Options Processing
sections.content:
Geneve options are intended to be originated and processed by tunnel endpoints, but options MAY be interpreted by transit devices along the tunnel path. Transit devices that do not interpret Geneve headers MUST handle Geneve packets as any other UDP packet and maintain consistent forwarding behavior. In tunnel endpoints, the generation and interpretation of options is determined by the control plane, which is beyond the scope of the document, but several requirements are imposed to ensure interoperability between heterogeneous devices.

Receiving tunnel endpoints MUST drop packets containing unknown options with the critical bit set, while transit devices MUST NOT drop packets as a result of encountering unknown options, including those with the critical bit set. The contents of the options and their ordering MUST NOT be modified by transit devices. If a tunnel endpoint receives a Geneve packet whose total option length exceeds its own options-processing capability, it MUST drop the packet, and the control plane is responsible for making sure the communicating peer tunnel endpoints have the capability to handle it.

When designing an option it is important to consider how it will evolve. Architecturally, options are intended to be self descriptive and independent, which enables parallelism in options processing and reduces implementation complexity, though the control plane may impose ordering restrictions. Unexpectedly significant interoperability issues may result from changing the length of an option that was defined to be a certain size. An option is specified to have either a fixed length, which is constant, or a variable length, and that property is part of the definition and is conveyed by the Type. Options that are defined to be a fixed length in size MUST NOT be redefined to a different length; a new Type should be allocated instead. The option type and its interpretation should be defined by the entity that owns the option class.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the tunnel endpoints are allowed to add or change options. A device in the middle may look at them, but it must pass them through untouched, and it must not drop a packet just because it does not understand an option.

sections.title: Deployment and Operation
sections.content:
Geneve is a UDP-based network virtualization overlay encapsulation protocol designed to establish tunnels between NVEs over an existing IP network. It is intended for use in public or private data center environments, for deploying multi-tenant overlay networks over an existing IP underlay network. It is intended to be deployed in a data center network environment operated by a single operator or an adjacent set of cooperating operators, which fits the definition of a controlled environment. The RFC defines a traffic-managed controlled environment as an IP network that is traffic engineered or otherwise managed, for example with traffic rate limiters, to avoid congestion.

Geneve does not natively provide congestion-control functionality and relies on the payload protocol traffic for congestion control. It MUST therefore be used with congestion-controlled traffic or within a traffic-managed controlled environment.

On encapsulation in IP, it is RECOMMENDED that Path MTU Discovery be used to prevent or minimize fragmentation. When determining the MTU size of a tunnel link, the maximum length of options MUST be assumed, as options may vary on a per-packet basis. For DSCP and ECN bits, the mechanism for exposing ECN capabilities on IP tunnels and propagating congestion markers to the inner packets MUST be followed, and the Pipe model for TTL is RECOMMENDED because it is more consistent with network virtualization.

Inner VLAN handling is OPTIONAL, and the processing of inner VLAN tags on ingress or egress is based on the configuration of the tunnel endpoint and the control plane, not defined as part of the data format. A Geneve tunnel is generally a unidirectional concept, and implementations MAY model tunnels as connected, bidirectional links, for example to provide the abstraction of a virtual port.

Modern NICs provide offloads that improve packet processing. Because Large Segmentation Offload and Large Receive Offload involve processing of the options themselves, since they must be replicated or merged across multiple packets, some constraints are placed on the definition of options: when performing LSO a NIC MUST replicate the entire Geneve header and all options, including unknown ones, onto each resulting segment unless an option allows an exception; options MUST NOT be reordered during offload processing, including when merging packets for LRO; and NICs performing offloads MUST NOT drop packets with unknown options, including critical ones, unless explicitly configured to do so.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sets out how Geneve behaves in a real data center: which checksums to use, how to avoid fragmenting packets, and what a network card may do with the options when it splits or merges packets in hardware.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As it is encapsulated within a UDP/IP packet, Geneve does not have any inherent security mechanisms. An attacker with access to the underlay network transporting the IP packets can snoop on, alter or inject packets, and compromised tunnel endpoints or transit devices may spoof identifiers in the tunnel header to gain access to networks owned by other tenants.

Within a particular security domain, such as a data center operated by a single service provider, the most common and highest-performing security mechanism is isolation of trusted components. Tunnel traffic can be carried over a separate VLAN and filtered at any untrusted boundaries. When crossing an untrusted link, such as the general Internet, VPN technologies such as IPsec SHOULD be used to provide authentication and encryption of the IP packets formed as part of Geneve encapsulation. Any Geneve overlay data leaving the data center network beyond the operator's security domain SHOULD be secured by encryption mechanisms.

If an operator determines data confidentiality is necessary, an encryption mechanism SHOULD be used to encrypt the tenant data end to end between the NVEs, and the NVEs may use existing well-established mechanisms such as IPsec or DTLS.

For data integrity, an NVE MUST NOT propagate Geneve packets beyond the NVE to tenant systems and SHOULD employ packet-filtering mechanisms so as not to forward unauthorized traffic between tenant systems in different tenant networks, and an NVE MUST NOT interpret Geneve packets from tenant systems other than as frames to be encapsulated. Malicious tampering of Geneve header fields may cause a packet from one tenant to be forwarded to a different tenant network, so a data integrity mechanism SHOULD be used in such environments.

To authenticate peers, an operator SHOULD use an authentication mechanism, such as IPsec, to ensure that the Geneve packet originated from the intended NVE peer. Where the packet is protected by encryption from tunnel endpoint to tunnel endpoint, transit devices have no visibility into the Geneve header or options and MUST handle Geneve packets as any other IP packet. Control plane communications between a Network Virtualization Authority and the NVEs are also expected to be protected, though the mechanisms are beyond the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Geneve itself does not protect anything. Inside one data center the usual answer is to keep the underlay separate and trusted, and across the public Internet the answer is to add IPsec or another VPN on top.

fields.desc: 3 reserved bits and a 5-bit length in 4-byte multiples, excluding the option header.

items.title: Control plane independence
items.text: Geneve is a pure tunnel format that explicitly selects no control plane.

items.text: Tunnel endpoints and transit devices must both be able to handle the protocol in hardware and in software.
